While this disparity between cities with and without physical limitations is a relevant point, there are significant problems with increasing the mileage formula by an arbitrary amount. For example, cities such as Boston, Baltimore, and Duluth, Minn., have physical limitations, but these limitations account for significantly less than 50 percent of the 360 degrees available for concentric diffusion. On the other hand, cities such as Miami, Norfolk-Newport News, Va., and San Francisco, have physical limitations which account for significantly more than 50 percent of the 360 degrees available for expansion. It is, therefore, apparent that a uniform arbitrary increase for cities having physical limitations will not achieve the same result for all cities.
Secondly, the exact meaning of the term "physical limitation" would have to be clearly defined. It is obvious that a large body of water such as an ocean, bay, or lake, constitutes a physical limitation. There are also situations where a mountain range, (as in Denver or El Paso) or a desert (as in Phoenix or Tuscon) may also be described as a physical limitation, although various techniques can accommodate diffusion in these areas. There are also cities, such as Miami, which are bordered by public parklands and marshlands (the Everglades). These constitute a physical limitation in the same manner as an ocean does inasmuch as development and, consequently, diffusion is severely restricted.

Use of Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas or Standard Consolidated Statistical Areas - As an alternative to the population-mileage formula, it has been suggested that the Commission utilize SMSA's and SCSA's to define commercial zones. The general concept of a metropolitan area is one of an integrated economic and social unit with a recognized large population nucleus...each standard metropolitan statistical area must contain at least 50,000 inhabitants ...
